name: Paleo diet

image.caption: Healthy Food Paleo Diet Primal Eating - Must link to https://thoroughlyreviewed.com

lead: The paleo diet builds meals from meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit and nuts and avoids grains, dairy, legumes and processed foods. It is popular in fitness and appearance communities as a whole-food route to leanness and clearer skin.

The chain: cutting processed food and several food groups lowers calorie intake, which researchers note is the main explanation for weight loss on the diet, and leads to a leaner body composition. Short trials report some metabolic changes. Wikipedia describes the research quality as poor to moderate, trials are small and short, and some anthropologists dispute the premise that it reflects how ancestral humans ate.

paras: People eat meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit and nuts, cook most meals themselves and skip bread, pasta, dairy and packaged foods. It is typically followed as a long-term eating style, with changes in body composition showing over weeks to months.
Reported concerns include lower calcium and vitamin D intake, side effects such as headaches and diarrhoea in one trial, and the cardiovascular associations of high red meat intake.

chain: Whole foods, no grains or dairy
angle.text: Followers adopt paleo eating for a leaner physique and less inflammation, built on meat, vegetables, fruit and nuts. Cutting processed foods, grains and dairy lowers calorie intake, which is the route to leaner body composition. Short trials report some metabolic changes.

lead: The Paleolithic or paleo diet is an eating pattern based on foods its proponents believe pre-agricultural humans ate. It emphasises vegetables, fruit, nuts, roots and meat, and excludes dairy, grains, legumes, refined sugar, processed oils and often salt and alcohol [1].

Versions of the idea date to the 1890s, and it was popularised by Walter Voegtlin in 1975, by Stanley Boyd Eaton and Melvin Konner from 1985, and by Loren Cordain, who trademarked the name in 2002 [1]. In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a whole-food, low-processed approach to skin, leanness and body composition. Wikipedia describes the research quality as poor to moderate, and critics including anthropologists dispute its assumptions about ancestral diets [1][2].
infobox: Walter Voegtlin (1975), S. Boyd Eaton and Melvin Konner (1985), Loren Cordain (2002)
Grains, dairy, legumes, refined sugar, processed oils

paras: The diet avoids processed food and builds meals around meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit and nuts. Dairy is excluded because milking began with animal domestication, and grains and legumes are excluded as agricultural foods [1]. Variants differ on the proportion of animal products: the 1988 Eaton, Konner and Shostak version was around 65% plant-based, while Cordain's later version emphasised animal foods [1].

Wikipedia traces precursors to Emmet Densmore and John Harvey Kellogg in the 1890s, Arnold DeVries in 1952, and Richard Mackarness's low-carbohydrate book in 1958. Voegtlin's 1975 The Stone Age Diet argued that humans were meat-eaters until about 10,000 years ago. The 1985 New England Journal of Medicine article by Eaton and Konner proposed the discordance hypothesis, that a mismatch between modern diets and human biology drives chronic disease [1]. The diet became widely popular online in the 2010s and was reported as Google's most searched weight-loss method in 2013 and 2014 [1].

A small metabolically controlled trial in type 2 diabetes compared a Paleolithic-type diet with a diabetes diet and reported metabolic differences over a short period [3]. A review of popular weight-loss strategies noted limited studies supporting fad diets, including paleo [2]. Wikipedia summarises a trial in obese postmenopausal women in which weight and fat loss at six months had disappeared by 24 months, and reviews that found no good evidence of reduced cardiovascular or metabolic syndrome risk [1]. Clinical statements and network meta-analyses have also compared dietary patterns on health biomarkers [4][5].

Anthropologists such as Peter Ungar and Marlene Zuk, and a 2018 analysis by Herman Pontzer and colleagues, have argued that ancestral diets varied widely, often included starchy plants, and that human evolution continued after agriculture [1]. Nutrition researcher Marion Nestle has said the evidence for ancestral diets is circumstantial [1].
Reported concerns include lower calcium and vitamin D intake, side effects such as weakness and headaches in one trial, and the cardiovascular associations of high red meat intake [1].

lore.intro: Proponents present the diet as a return to unprocessed whole foods; the community material is limited, so the claims below follow the standard proponent and expert positions.

claims.claim: Humans are genetically adapted to a pre-agricultural diet, so grains and dairy cause modern disease.
Paleo eating improves leanness and body composition.
The diet treats autoimmune and inflammatory disease.

timeline.event: Walter Voegtlin publishes The Stone Age Diet [1].
Eaton and Konner publish their discordance hypothesis in the New England Journal of Medicine [1].
Loren Cordain publishes The Paleo Diet and trademarks the name [1].
Paleo reported as Google's top-searched weight-loss method [1].
